_note: The LED lesson of the learning journey (TRD addendum sections 4, 5 and 6.1). It fixes the reference circuit of Arduino Foundations level 2 with a version number. Change the version when the circuit, the code or the map changes. baseline.levels: the levels of content/boards/arduino-foundations.json that make the reference board. The reference code is the solution of the level 2 code step in content/sketches/arduino-foundations.json. map: one item for each terminal and each connection; the id is the stable id. The explain text tells the holes of the reference build. changes: the changes that the simulator shows correctly (supported: true, a challenge can use them), and two that it cannot show (supported: false, with the reason). ops changes the reference; model is what the simulator then shows. tests/observe.test.ts runs each change. schematic: the id of the element in components/journey/schematic-af-led.tsx that shows the terminal or the connection (Compare views, issue #202). The lesson has no media and no questions until the photos and the clip of the real circuit exist; lib/journey/questions.ts gives the shape of a question. The challenges come in work package 6. Write the text in ASD-STE100.

inventory.name: Wire from GND to the − line
Wire from pin 13 to the resistor
Wire from the LED to the − line

terminals.label: + line on the left of breadboard A
− line on the left of breadboard A

connections.explain: A wire takes 5 V from the Uno to the + line on the left of breadboard A. The 25 holes of this line connect inside the breadboard.
A wire connects GND of the Uno to the − line on the left of breadboard A. The 25 holes of this line connect inside the breadboard, so a part that touches the line touches ground.
A wire takes pin 13 to hole a22 of breadboard A. Holes a to e of column 22 connect inside the breadboard. The first leg of the resistor is in hole c22, so pin 13 touches the resistor.
The second leg of the resistor is in hole c26, and the long leg (+) of the LED is in hole e26. Holes a to e of column 26 connect inside the breadboard, so this connection needs no wire.
The short leg (−) of the LED is in hole e27. A wire goes from hole a27 to the − line, and the − line goes to GND. This closes the loop from pin 13 back to the Uno.

ref.title: Reference photo
ref.alt: A real circuit on a white table. A white breadboard is on the left and a red SparkFun RedBoard is on the right. A yellow wire goes from pin 13 of the board to the breadboard. A resistor goes from the line of the yellow wire to the line of a red LED. A black wire goes from the other line of the LED to a GND pin of the board.
ref.note: This photo shows a SparkFun RedBoard. Its pins are the same as the pins of the Arduino Uno. The resistor in the photo is 330 Ω, and the lesson uses 220 Ω. The circuit is the same: pin 13, resistor, LED, GND. The black wire goes directly to the GND pin, so this photo does not use the − line. The two legs of the LED are near each other in this photo.

layout2.title: A different layout
layout2.alt: A real circuit on a black plate. A blue Arduino Uno is at the back and a white breadboard is at the front. A red wire goes from pin 13 of the Uno to the line of the long leg of a yellow LED. The LED is on. A resistor goes from the line of the short leg of the LED to the − line of the breadboard. A black wire goes from the − line to a GND pin of the Uno.
layout2.note: This is the same loop in a different layout, on an Arduino Uno. Here the resistor is after the LED: pin 13, LED, resistor, − line, GND. The order of the parts in one loop does not change the current. The resistor in the photo is 330 Ω.

notes.c-d13-r1: In this layout, the wire from pin 13 goes to the long leg (+) of the LED, not to the resistor. The resistor is after the LED.
notes.c-r1-led: In this layout, the resistor touches the short leg (−) of the LED, not the long leg.
notes.c-led-gnd: In this layout, the short leg (−) of the LED goes through the resistor to the − line. Then the black wire goes from the − line to GND.

changes.text: Move the end of the pin 13 wire to pin 12.
Remove the wire from the LED to the − line.
Move the end of the LED wire from the − line to the + line.
Move the short leg (−) of the LED to the + line.
Put the resistor on the other side of the LED: pin 13 to the LED, then the resistor, then the − line.
Change each delay(500) in the sketch to delay(100).
Remove the resistor, and join its two holes with a wire.
changes.reason: The simulator shows the LED blink, but a real LED gets too much current and can burn. The simulator does not calculate current.

changes.text: A wire is loose in its hole.
changes.reason: In the simulator, a wire is in its hole or it is not. A real loose wire makes the LED flicker or stay off. Use the fault clip for this change.

challenges.title: Take away the wire to ground

options.text: Current flows only in a closed loop. Without this wire, the path from pin 13 does not get back to GND. Thus no current flows through the LED.
options.feedback: Correct. Current needs a full loop: out of pin 13, through the resistor and the LED, and back to GND. When the loop is open at one point, the current is zero in each part.

options.text: Pin 13 still sends current into the LED. The current stops at the end of the LED, where it has no more room.
options.feedback: Current does not flow into a dead end. The long leg of the LED still has voltage from pin 13, but current flows only when the loop is closed. With the loop open, the current is zero in each part, also before the LED.

options.text: Pin 13 senses that the wire is not there, and the Uno turns its output off.
options.feedback: The Uno does not know what you connect. Pin 13 continues to go HIGH and LOW each half second. The LED is off because the loop is open, not because the pin is off.

hints.text: Follow the path with your finger. Start at pin 13 and try to get back to GND.
Electric current needs a full loop. Find the place where the path stops.
Look at the short leg (−) of the LED. The wire that you removed took it to GND. Without that wire, the loop is open.

variation.text: This is a circuit in other holes. The wire to the − line is in column 16. The short leg (−) of the LED is in column 15.

options.text: Holes a to e connect only in the same column. The wire is in column 16 and the LED leg is in column 15. Thus the loop is open.
options.feedback: Correct. Column 15 and column 16 are separate inside the breadboard. The wire touches nothing, so the path from the LED does not get back to GND.

options.text: Holes that are side by side always connect. Thus the loop is closed.
options.feedback: Only the 5 holes a to e of the same column connect inside the breadboard. Column 15 and column 16 are side by side, but they are separate. The loop is open.

options.text: The wire goes to the − line, so the loop is closed. The LED is off because the parts are too far from the Uno.
options.feedback: Distance does not matter here. One end of the wire is in the − line, but its other end is not in the column of the LED leg. The loop is open.

options.text: An LED lets current through in one direction only: in at the long leg (+), out at the short leg (−). Turned around, it blocks the current.
options.feedback: Correct. An LED is a diode. It is like a one-way door for current. When the long leg (+) is on the side of GND, the door is closed and no current flows.

options.text: The LED works in both directions. Turned around, it gives a light that is too weak to see.
options.feedback: A reversed LED does not give a weak light. It blocks the current, so it gives no light. Only a resistor that is too large makes an LED dim.

options.text: The resistor is now on the wrong side of the LED, so it stops all the current.
options.feedback: The resistor did not move. A resistor also works the same in both directions. The LED is the part that has a direction.

hints.text: Look at the two legs of the LED. They are not the same.
The long leg is +. Current goes in at the long leg and out at the short leg. Which leg is on the side of pin 13 now?
The resistor now touches the short leg (−) of the LED. Current cannot go in at the short leg.

variation.text: In this layout the LED points to the left. Its long leg (+) is in column 12, with the resistor. Its short leg (−) is in column 11, with the wire to the − line.

options.text: Left or right on the board is not important. The long leg (+) is on the side of pin 13 and the short leg (−) is on the side of GND. Thus current can flow.
options.feedback: Correct. Polarity is about the legs, not about the direction on the board. Current comes from pin 13 through the resistor into the long leg (+), and goes out at the short leg (−) to GND.

options.text: The LED points to the left, so it is reversed and it blocks the current.
options.feedback: The direction on the board does not make an LED reversed. Follow the path: pin 13, resistor, long leg (+), short leg (−), GND. The current goes in at the long leg, so the LED lights.

options.text: An LED works in both directions, so it always lights.
options.feedback: An LED works in one direction only. It lights here because its long leg (+) is on the side of pin 13. If you turn it around, it stays off.

challenges.title: Put the resistor after the LED

options.text: The resistor and the LED are in one path, in series. The current is the same at each point of one path. Thus the resistor limits the current on each side of the LED.
options.feedback: Correct. In a series path, the same current goes through each part. The sequence of the parts does not change the current, so the LED blinks as before and it is as safe as before.

options.text: The LED now gets the full current first. The resistor comes too late to protect it.
options.feedback: Current is not used up along the path, and it does not get to one part first. In one series path, the current is the same in each part. The resistor limits it for the full path.

options.text: Pin 13 goes directly to the LED now, so the resistor has no function in this position.
options.feedback: The resistor still limits the current. Without a resistor, a real LED gets too much current and can burn. Its position in the series path does not change its function.

hints.text: Count the paths from pin 13 to GND. Is there one path, or are there more?
In one path, the same current goes through each part, one after the other.
Start at pin 13. The path now goes through the LED first, then through the resistor, then to GND. It is still one path.

variation.text: In this layout the resistor goes directly from the short leg (−) of the LED into the − line. There is no wire between the resistor and the − line.

options.text: It is still one closed path: pin 13, LED, resistor, GND. A leg of a part can do the work of a wire.
options.feedback: Correct. The leg of the resistor is metal, as a wire is. It connects the resistor to the − line. The path is closed and it is in series, so the LED blinks.

options.text: The resistor is in the − line, so both its legs touch GND and no current goes through it.
options.feedback: Only one leg of the resistor is in the − line. The other leg is in column 9, with the short leg of the LED. The LED current goes through the resistor to GND.

options.text: The − line must get a wire, not a part. The loop is open.
options.feedback: A hole takes a wire or a leg of a part. Both are metal and both connect. The loop is closed.
